title: TCP U1·W2 — Deductions, Credits, QBI & AMT (2026)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — turning the formula into savings

With gross income and AGI set (Week 1), the next levers are itemized deductions, the qualified business income (QBI) deduction, and credits — plus the alternative minimum tax (AMT) that can claw back the benefit of aggressive planning. This is where the largest individual savings are won, and where the 2026 Public Law 119-21 baseline differs most sharply from older rules. The planner's job is to maximize the deductions and credits that survive the current law and to avoid the AMT trap.

Itemized deductions in 2026

The major itemized deductions carry specific 2026 limits. State and local taxes (SALT) are capped at $40,400 for 2026 (up from $40,000 in 2025), with a MAGI-based phasedown toward a $10,000 floor for high earners and half that for MFS (§70120) — a major change from the old flat $10,000. Home-mortgage interest is deductible on up to $750,000 of acquisition debt (made permanent; pre-2018 loans grandfathered at $1,000,000). Medical expenses are deductible only above 7.5% of AGI. Casualty losses are limited to federally declared disasters and, for years after 2025, qualifying state-declared disasters. Critically, miscellaneous 2%-of-AGI deductions are permanently terminated (§70110) — unreimbursed employee expenses and investment fees no longer deduct.

Charitable contributions

Charitable contributions are a flexible planning tool, deductible up to AGI percentage ceilings — generally 60% of AGI for cash gifts to public charities and 30% for appreciated long-term capital-gain property (deducted at fair value, avoiding tax on the appreciation). Excess contributions carry forward five years. Donating appreciated stock rather than cash is a classic move — the donor deducts full value and never recognizes the gain. Bunching gifts (Week 1) or using a donor-advised fund lets a taxpayer clear the standard deduction in alternating years while smoothing the actual giving.

The QBI deduction

The §199A qualified business income (QBI) deduction — made permanent under the 2026 baseline — lets owners of pass-through businesses (sole proprietorships, partnerships, S corporations) deduct up to 20% of qualified business income, a powerful benefit for an owner like Jordan Reed. Above income thresholds, the deduction is limited by the greater of 50% of W-2 wages or 25% of wages plus 2.5% of qualified property, and is phased out for specified service trades or businesses (SSTBs) (law, health, consulting, accounting). A core planning question is structuring the business and compensation to preserve the 20% deduction — for example, paying enough W-2 wages to satisfy the wage limit.

Tax credits

Credits reduce tax dollar-for-dollar (more valuable than deductions) and split into nonrefundable (limited to tax owed) and refundable (paid even beyond tax). Key individual credits: the child tax credit (for qualifying children, with a refundable portion), the child and dependent care credit, the education credits — the American Opportunity Tax Credit (AOTC) (partly refundable, first four years of college) and the Lifetime Learning Credit — the retirement savings (saver's) credit, the earned income tax credit (EITC), and the foreign tax credit. Because credits phase out by income, managing AGI (Week 1) can preserve credit eligibility.

The alternative minimum tax

The alternative minimum tax (AMT) is a parallel tax system ensuring high-income taxpayers pay a minimum. It starts from taxable income, adds back certain preferences and adjustments (e.g., the standard deduction, certain interest, incentive-stock-option bargain elements), subtracts an AMT exemption (which phases out at high income), and applies the AMT rate; the taxpayer pays the greater of regular tax or AMT. Because the SALT and miscellaneous deductions that once triggered AMT are now capped or eliminated, far fewer individuals owe AMT under the current baseline — but incentive stock options and certain other items still create AMT exposure that planning must anticipate.

Other taxes and the planning synthesis

Two surtaxes complete the picture. The net investment income tax (NIIT) adds 3.8% on investment income for higher earners, and the additional Medicare tax adds 0.9% on wages and self-employment income above thresholds. The planning synthesis: reduce AGI to relax phaseouts and surtaxes, maximize the QBI deduction and surviving itemized deductions, harvest credits, and avoid AMT triggers — all coordinated across years. For a business owner, the entity structure (next weeks) interacts with every one of these, which is why TCP treats individual and entity planning as one integrated problem. Sequencing the moves — adjustments first, then deductions, then credits — captures each benefit before the next income-based phaseout bites.

Education and retirement tax incentives

The code offers targeted incentives a planner harvests. For education, beyond the AOTC and Lifetime Learning credits, 529 plans grow tax-free for qualified education expenses and Coverdell ESAs offer a smaller alternative. For retirement, traditional accounts deduct now and defer tax while Roth accounts forgo the deduction for tax-free withdrawals later — a bracket bet (Roth wins if future rates are higher), and timing a Roth conversion into a low-income year fills low brackets cheaply. An HSA is triple tax-advantaged (deductible in, tax-free growth, tax-free for medical), doubling as a stealth retirement account. Choosing traditional versus Roth and funding education accounts early interact with the same AGI and bracket management from Week 1.

Coordinating deductions across years

Because only itemized deductions above the enhanced standard deduction yield a benefit, coordination across years matters. Bunching clusters charitable gifts and elective medical procedures into a single year to itemize, then takes the standard deduction the next — a donor-advised fund makes this seamless, funding several years of giving at once while distributing to charities over time. The SALT cap reshapes the calculus: with state taxes limited, charitable and mortgage-interest deductions do more of the work of clearing the standard deduction, so their timing carries extra weight in a multi-year plan. Mapping three years of expected income and deductions together, rather than optimizing one year in isolation, is what separates planning from compliance.

CMA bridge

For MBG's owner, the QBI deduction and the SALT cap directly shape after-tax income, and the choice to pay W-2 wages versus take distributions affects both the QBI wage limit and payroll taxes. The CFO who models these together — entity tax, owner's QBI, payroll, and the surtaxes — finds the structure that minimizes the family's total tax, the integrative skill TCP rewards.

Practice and recap

  1. Apply 2026 itemized limits: SALT cap $40,400 (phasedown to $10k floor), $750k mortgage acquisition debt, medical > 7.5% AGI, casualty federal/state-declared; misc 2% deductions terminated.
  2. Plan charitable gifts (60% AGI cash / 30% appreciated property at FMV; 5-year carryforward; donate appreciated stock; bunch / donor-advised funds).
  3. Maximize the §199A QBI deduction (20%, permanent; wage/property limits and SSTB phaseout above thresholds).
  4. Use credits (child, AOTC/LLC, dependent care, saver's, EITC, foreign tax); anticipate AMT (ISOs) and the 3.8% NIIT / 0.9% additional Medicare surtaxes.

Recap: 2026 itemized deductions feature a SALT cap of $40,400 (phasing toward a $10,000 floor), $750,000 mortgage-acquisition-debt interest, a 7.5%-of-AGI medical floor, and disaster-only casualty losses, with miscellaneous 2% deductions permanently gone; charitable gifts deduct up to 60% (cash) or 30% (appreciated property at fair value) of AGI; the permanent §199A QBI deduction shields up to 20% of pass-through income subject to wage/property limits and SSTB phaseouts; and credits beat deductions dollar-for-dollar while the AMT and the 3.8% NIIT / 0.9% Medicare surtaxes are the traps a planner steers around.

flashcards.back: $40,400 for 2026 ($40,000 in 2025), with a MAGI phasedown toward a $10,000 floor (half for MFS) — §70120. Not the old flat $10,000.
Permanently terminated (§70110) — unreimbursed employee expenses, investment/advisory fees no longer deductible.
Mortgage interest on up to $750k acquisition debt (permanent; pre-2018 grandfathered $1M). Medical > 7.5% AGI. Casualty: federally declared + (after 2025) state-declared disasters only.
Cash to public charity: up to 60% of AGI. Appreciated LT capital-gain property: up to 30% of AGI, deducted at fair value (no gain recognized). Excess carries forward 5 years.
Up to 20% of qualified business income from pass-throughs (permanent in 2026). Above thresholds: limited by 50% of W-2 wages (or 25% wages + 2.5% property); phased out for SSTBs.
Nonrefundable: limited to tax owed (e.g., LLC, dependent care, foreign tax). Refundable: paid beyond tax (EITC; partly the child credit and AOTC).
Parallel system: taxable income + preferences/adjustments (ISO bargain element, etc.) − AMT exemption (phases out) × AMT rate; pay the GREATER of regular tax or AMT. Fewer owe it now (SALT capped).
NIIT: 3.8% on net investment income above thresholds. Additional Medicare: 0.9% on wages/SE income above thresholds.

questions.q: Under the 2026 baseline, the SALT deduction cap is:
choices: $40,400, with a MAGI phasedown toward a $10,000 floor
questions.explain: PL 119-21 §70120 sets the 2026 SALT cap at $40,400 with a high-income phasedown to $10,000.

questions.q: The §199A QBI deduction generally allows pass-through owners to deduct up to:
questions.explain: QBI is up to 20% of qualified business income, subject to wage/property limits and SSTB phaseouts.

questions.q: Donating appreciated long-term stock to charity lets the donor:
choices: Deduct fair value and avoid recognizing the gain (up to 30% of AGI)
questions.explain: Appreciated LTCG property is deducted at fair value (30%-of-AGI limit) with no gain recognized.

questions.q: A taxpayer pays the AMT when:
choices: Tentative minimum tax exceeds the regular tax
AGI is below the standard deduction
questions.explain: AMT is owed when the tentative minimum tax exceeds the regular tax — you pay the greater.

questions.q: The net investment income tax (NIIT) rate is:
questions.explain: NIIT adds 3.8% on net investment income above income thresholds; the 0.9% is the additional Medicare tax on earned income.

questions.q: Credits are generally more valuable than deductions because they:
questions.explain: A credit reduces the tax itself dollar-for-dollar; a deduction only reduces taxable income.
